note: The report page's glossary, as DATA (unit READ-A; owner ruling AC41(5), the owner's finding 2 of 2026-09-25; architect ruling 5 on the READ-A bracket). Each note is one plain sentence, with the calculation where there is one. 'tape' holds the note for each row of the market-data table, keyed by the first figure the row shows. 'terms' holds the words a key-number label or a metric name in the chairman's tables may carry; the page marks the first place each term appears in such a label and shows the note when the mouse rests on it, or on a tap on a phone. 'series' names the rate and credit series of the cycle in plain words, keyed by the series' own code. 'models' gives a model's plain name for the stamp under the rating (an id not listed prints as recorded); 'benchmarks' names a benchmark fund for the chart's caption.

tape_all_days.tape_return_21: The price change over the last 30 days, about a month (a coin trades every day); the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape_all_days.tape_return_63: The price change over the last 91 days, about three months (a coin trades every day); the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape_all_days.tape_return_126: The price change over the last 183 days, about six months (a coin trades every day); the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape_all_days.tape_return_252: The price change over the last 365 days, about a year (a coin trades every day); the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape_all_days.tape_realized_vol_21: How much the price has swung day to day, scaled to a year: the standard deviation of the daily returns over each window, times the square root of 365, because a coin trades every day.
tape_all_days.tape_high_close_252: The highest and the lowest daily close of the last 365 days, with the day each was set.
tape_all_days.tape_closes_above_sma200_252: How often the coin closed above its 200-day average over the last year: the number of the last 365 closes above the average of the 200 closes ending that day.

tape.tape_close_vs_sma50: How far the last close sits above or below the average of the last 50 daily closes: last close divided by that average, less one, as a percentage.
tape.tape_close_vs_sma100: How far the last close sits above or below the average of the last 100 daily closes: last close divided by that average, less one, as a percentage.
tape.tape_close_vs_sma200: How far the last close sits above or below the average of the last 200 daily closes: last close divided by that average, less one, as a percentage.
tape.tape_sma200_slope_60: Whether the long-run trend is rising or falling: today's 200-day average divided by the 200-day average of 60 trading days ago, less one, as a percentage.
tape.tape_range_place_252: Where the last close sits between the lowest and highest close of the last year: last close less the lowest, divided by the highest less the lowest (0% is the low, 100% the high).
tape.tape_drawdown_from_high_252: How far the last close is below the highest close of the last year: last close divided by that high, less one, as a percentage.
tape.tape_return_21: The price change over the last 21 trading days, about a month; the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape.tape_return_63: The price change over the last 63 trading days, about three months; the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape.tape_return_126: The price change over the last 126 trading days, about six months; the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape.tape_return_252: The price change over the last 252 trading days, about a year; the second figure is that change less the benchmark's change over the same days, in percentage points.
tape.tape_realized_vol_21: How much the price has swung day to day, scaled to a year: the standard deviation of the daily returns over each window, times the square root of 252.
tape.tape_volume_20_vs_250: Whether trading is busier or quieter than usual: the average daily volume of the last 20 days divided by that of the last 250 days.
tape.tape_largest_fall_252: The worst single day of the last year: the largest fall from one close to the next, as a percentage.
tape.tape_high_close_252: The highest and the lowest daily close of the last 252 trading days, with the day each was set.
tape.tape_closes_above_sma200_252: How often the stock closed above its 200-day average over the last year: the number of the last 252 closes above the average of the 200 closes ending that day.

terms.note: The yearly dividend on the stated amount, divided by today's price.
How many times the company's coins and cash would pay every claim ranking ahead of this share and alongside it.
The amount per share the dividend rate is paid on, and the amount the share ranks for.
Not paid on its date but still owed: the share's missed dividends accumulate.
Not paid and never to be paid.
Every debt, and every preferred share the filings rank ahead of this one, paid first.

terms.term: Premium or discount to its coins
terms.note: How far the share's market value sits above the coins at today's price, plus cash, less the true debt, as a share of that value. Below it is a discount.
The coins the company owns divided by its shares. It rises when new shares sell above the treasury's value and falls when they sell below it.
The yearly interest on the company's bonds and loans, and the dividends on its preferred shares. The council counts how many months its cash covers them without selling coin.
The coin price at which the true debt equals the coins plus cash: below it the common share owns no coin. Calculated from the recorded figures.
A loan secured on the coins that the lender may call by selling them. The front page names any the company has.
A listed fund that owns the coin itself, priced against its own net asset value. Buying the coin through it is the plain alternative to this share.
Worked out by the council from the recorded figures, never estimated, and shown beside the figures it rests on.
The price for uranium delivered now, in US dollars a pound. The council works it out daily: the Sprott trust's uranium value divided by its pounds.
The price power companies agree now for uranium delivered in later years under long contracts. It is published monthly; a producer's reserves are compared with it.
A listed trust or company whose value is the uranium it owns in store. The council sits uranium through one, because it is what the owner could actually buy.
The value of the holder's uranium and cash, less what it owes, per share, as the holder itself publishes it. The council never works out its own.
How far the share price sits below the holder's own published value per share; a price above it is a premium. Shown beside its level at the last five year-ends.
Uranium is counted in pounds of uranium oxide, the form mines sell. A company reporting tonnes of uranium is converted at one fixed published factor, 2,599.8 pounds a tonne.
The uranium a producer has already agreed to sell in future years, shown exactly as the company publishes it: year by year, an average, a total, or not published.
The rating judges three years, not twelve months, for uranium alone: its contracting cycle runs longer than a year. The expected return is set yearly against cash.
The change in the pounds the physical holders own over one, three and twelve months. The twelve-month change is set against the two largest miners' guided output this year.
The money an insurer keeps between collecting premiums and paying claims. It belongs to policyholders, but the insurer invests it in the meantime.

An insurer that invests its float largely in shares and in businesses it owns outright: together they are more than a third of its assets, or it reports those businesses as segments of their own. Its book value grows from underwriting and investing together.

terms.term: Book value per share growth with dividends added back
terms.note: How fast book value per share grew each year between the first and last year-ends shown, counting the dividends paid in between as if kept: latest book value per share plus those dividends, divided by the first, then the yearly compound rate.

The company's own published figure that restates its book value, such as its net asset value per share, or book value plus its own fair-value adjustment. The council prints it in the company's words and never works one out itself.
Premiums earned less claims and the costs of writing the policies, for one year. Above zero means the insurance itself made a profit before any investment income.
The company's market value divided by its book value - common shareholders' equity at the latest quarter end. Above one, the market pays more than the books say the company is worth.
A low, middle and high value for the token, worked out by the machine from the fees that reach its holders, on the method the owner named.
Users' fees that reach token holders, by four routes only: tokens destroyed from fees; tokens bought back and destroyed or locked; fees paid to stakers; fees switched on by vote.
The chairman's one-word judgment of the next twelve months' new tokens: tailwind, neutral or headwind. It is his judgment, checked by the outside reviewer, with no fixed threshold.
Tokens that become free to trade in the window, whoever receives them, less tokens destroyed or bought back and locked; shown as a share of the tokens trading today.
A past token whose price fell hard as new supply reached the market, named by the owner; the chairman calls this token structurally similar, structurally different or in between.
A bull and a bear case for one and three months, each with a price range, a chance and its trigger. The council's judgment; it does not move the rating.
A price or value the owner names before the evidence. The chairman gives the chance it is reached at any point in twelve months, never below his ladder's year-end chance.
This figure comes from one service only, because no free second service carries it. It is used, and labelled so you can judge it.
The second fee service's figure differs from DefiLlama's by more than a quarter. Both are shown; the council works from DefiLlama's.
The release dates come from a data service, not the protocol itself. Accepted only where the protocol's own documents state the totals and the release rule.
The past case's release pace was measured on one trading-volume service; this token has no figure from that same service, so the two paces are not compared.
Holders receive no share of the fees today, so there is no fair-value range; the rating rests on the twelve-month price scenarios alone.
The owner's one stop before any advisor is paid: he reads the declared method, comparables, past case and claim, and approves or redirects. A protocol sitting always stops here.
A coin whose protocol can hide transaction details, including who paid whom and how much.
An exchange with a recorded licence in the United States, European Union or United Kingdom that lists this coin.
A named price outcome and probability for the case where regulated exchanges stop listing the coin.
The coins the recorded issuance schedule adds over the next thirty days, including a halving if it falls inside that window.
The value of one day’s new coins divided by the recorded thirty-day average daily trading value.
Return on tangible common equity: a year's profit to common shareholders divided by their equity less goodwill and other intangible assets, the main measure of a bank's profitability.
A year's profit to common shareholders divided by their equity less goodwill and other intangible assets, the main measure of a bank's profitability.
Common equity tier 1: a bank's core capital, shareholders' equity less intangibles and deductions, measured against its risk-weighted assets.
A bank's common equity tier 1 capital, shareholders' equity less intangibles and deductions, divided by its risk-weighted assets.
The bank's core capital ratio against the minimum its regulator requires of it; the gap is the cushion that pays for losses, dividends and buybacks.
Shareholders' equity less goodwill and other intangible assets, what the shareholders would own if the bank were wound up at book values.
The share price divided by tangible book value per share: what the market pays for each dollar of the bank's tangible equity.
The average of the last 200 daily closes, a common read of the long-run trend.
The price at which the chairman says the case reopens as a buy, provided the conditions he names still hold.
The lower price at which the chairman says more could be bought, provided the conditions he names still hold.
The latest traded price the evidence recorded, the price this ruling is made against.
Loans written off in the quarter, less what was recovered, as a yearly percentage of the average loans outstanding.
What bad loans cost the bank: loans written off and the provisions set aside for future losses.
The interest a bank earns on loans and securities less the interest it pays on deposits and borrowing.
The yearly return on a short US government bill, the cash rate a buyer could earn with no credit risk.
The day the company next reports its quarterly results, the next scheduled test of this rating.

The growth yardstick: what the whole business costs - the market value of its shares plus its debt, less its cash - divided by the last four quarters' gross profit, which is sales less the direct cost of making them.
Cash and short-term investments divided by the last four quarters' cash burn, counted in months; undrawn credit lines are shown but not counted.
The cash a company spends beyond what its operations bring in: capital spending less operating cash flow, over the last four quarters.
Pay to staff in shares or options instead of cash: a real cost that dilutes the shareholders, shown here as a share of sales.
The number of shares counting those that options, share awards and convertible debt would add, as the company counts them for its earnings per share.
The yearly value of the subscriptions a company has in force, by its own definition, not a figure of standard accounting.
The latest quarter's sales against the same quarter a year earlier, as a percentage change.
Oil and gas the company is reasonably certain to produce from known fields at the prices and costs of its reserve report, under the reporting standard it names; only its own share.
Metal a miner has shown, by drilling and a mine plan, it can extract at a profit at the price of its reserve report - the proven part more certain than the probable; only its own share.
One unit for oil and gas together: six thousand cubic feet of gas counted as one barrel of oil, the convention the filings use.
A miner's cost per ounce by the World Gold Council's definition: the cost of mining plus the spending needed to keep the mine producing, before growth projects.
The reserves divided by the last four quarters' output, counted in years - worked out by the council from the recorded figures.

terms.term: Price the reserves were counted at
terms.note: The commodity price the reserve report assumed when it counted the reserves, as its reporting standard sets it; today's price is shown beside it.

The US SEC's own figure for an oil and gas producer: the future cash from its proved reserves at the reserve report's prices, discounted at ten percent a year - shown beside the yardstick, never part of it.
The fixed price a streaming company pays for each ounce or barrel it receives under a stream agreement - its cost in place of a mining cost.
What the company owes to close its wells or mines and restore the land when they stop producing, as carried on its balance sheet.
The value of what the holding company owns, less its own net debt. The council uses today's listed prices and the company's latest private values.

How far the share price is below the value per share, or the market value below the total value. Today's prices give the discount rated; the company's published value gives the comparison with history.
The holding company's own net debt as a share of the gross value of what it owns, calculated from the recorded figures.
An investment in a business without a listed share price. The council takes the company's latest value, with its date and valuation basis.
The company's own latest published value, printed beside the council's value and used for the historical comparison.
Whether the dividends the holding company receives cover its own costs, interest and the dividend it pays.
